claim: Mitochondria evolved from a single endosymbiotic event between an ancestral alpha-proteobacterium and an archaeon-related host cell.
source: Mitochondria evolved from a single endosymbiotic event between an ancestral alpha-proteobacterium and an archaeon-related host cell.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on mitochondrial evolution.

claim: During the conversion of the endosymbiont into an organelle, most genes encoded in the genome of the proto-mitochondrion were either lost or transferred to the host genome.
source: During the gradual conversion of the endosymbiont into an organelle, most of the many genes encoded in the genome of the proto-mitochondrion were either lost or transferred to the host genome (Roger et al., 2017; Archibald, 2015; Dacks et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: Mitochondrial genes now encoded in the nucleus are translated on cytosolic ribosomes and imported into the various mitochondrial subcompartments.
source: The mitochondrial genes that are now encoded in the nucleus, are translated on cytosolic ribosomes and imported into the various mitochondrial subcompartments.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitochondrial protein import.

claim: Mitochondrial protein import is executed by several protein complexes that were thought to be well conserved.
source: Mitochondrial protein import is executed by several protein complexes, which were thought to be well conserved (Pfanner et al., 2019; Hansen and Herrmann, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on mitochondrial import machinery.

claim: Mitochondria can be traced back to the Last Eukaryotic Common Ancestor (LECA).
source: However, as mitochondria have a billion-year history and can be traced back to the Last Eukaryotic Common Ancestor (LECA) (Roger et al., 2017), it is difficult to gain unambiguous information about their origin and diversification.
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on eukaryotic evolution.

claim: Nearly all eukaryotes have mitochondria or related organelles.
source: Although (nearly Karnkowska et al., 2016) all eukaryotes have mitochondria or related organelles, recent studies have shown that mitochondria and their import apparatuses are considerably diverse (Dolezal et al., 2006; Harsman and Schneider, 2017; Mani et al., 2016; Gray, 2012; Fukasawa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations including one noting an exception.

claim: Mitochondria and their import apparatuses are considerably diverse.
source: Although (nearly Karnkowska et al., 2016) all eukaryotes have mitochondria or related organelles, recent studies have shown that mitochondria and their import apparatuses are considerably diverse (Dolezal et al., 2006; Harsman and Schneider, 2017; Mani et al., 2016; Gray, 2012; Fukasawa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent studies.

claim: The translocase of the outer membrane (TOM) complex in S. cerevisiae comprises seven subunits.
source: The translocase of the outer membrane (TOM) complex in S. cerevisiae comprises seven subunits, of which three are conserved across all eukaryotic lineages and can be traced to LECA (Mani et al., 2016; Maćasev et al., 2004; Mani et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on the TOM complex.

claim: Three subunits of the TOM complex are conserved across all eukaryotic lineages and can be traced to LECA.
source: The translocase of the outer membrane (TOM) complex in S. cerevisiae comprises seven subunits, of which three are conserved across all eukaryotic lineages and can be traced to LECA (Mani et al., 2016; Maćasev et al., 2004; Mani et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to comparative studies.

claim: The atypical translocase of the outer membrane (ATOM) in trypanosomes consists of seven subunits.
source: On the other hand, the atypical translocase of the outer membrane (ATOM) in trypanosomes also consists of seven subunits, but only two of these are shared with all eukaryotes (Mani et al., 2016; Mani et al., 2017; Mani et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on trypanosome ATOM complex.

claim: Only two subunits of the trypanosome ATOM complex are shared with all eukaryotes.
source: On the other hand, the atypical translocase of the outer membrane (ATOM) in trypanosomes also consists of seven subunits, but only two of these are shared with all eukaryotes (Mani et al., 2016; Mani et al., 2017; Mani et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to comparative studies.

claim: Most eukaryotes have two TIM complexes (TIM22 and TIM23) which do not have any subunits in common.
source: Most eukaryotes have two TIM complexes (TIM22 and TIM23) which do not have any subunits in common (Harsman and Schneider, 2017; Žárský and Doležal, 2016; Marom et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on TIM complexes.

claim: The TIM22 complex is specialized for membrane insertion of proteins that contain multiple membrane-spanning domains such as mitochondrial carrier proteins.
source: The TIM22 complex is specialized for membrane insertion of proteins that contain multiple membrane-spanning domains such as mitochondrial carrier proteins (Ferramosca and Zara, 2013; Pfanner and Neupert, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on TIM22 function.

claim: The TIM23 complex mediates membrane translocation and insertion of presequence-containing proteins.
source: The TIM23 complex mediates membrane translocation and insertion of presequence-containing proteins (Pfanner et al., 2019; Hansen and Herrmann, 2019; Marom et al., 2011; Mokranjac and Neupert, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on TIM23 function.

claim: Trypanosomes have only a single TIM complex that functions in both import of presequence-containing and carrier proteins.
source: Surprisingly, trypanosomes have only a single TIM complex that, with minor variations, functions in both import of presequence-containing and carrier proteins (Harsman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on trypanosome TIM complex.

claim: TbTim17 is the only TIM complex component shared between trypanosomes and other eukaryotes.
source: The only TIM complex component shared between trypanosomes and other eukaryotes is TbTim17 (Harsman et al., 2016; Singha et al., 2012), an orthologue of the Tim22 subunit of the TIM22 complex (Žárský and Doležal, 2016; Pyrihová et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on TIM complex components.

claim: TbTim17 is an orthologue of the Tim22 subunit of the TIM22 complex.
source: The only TIM complex component shared between trypanosomes and other eukaryotes is TbTim17 (Harsman et al., 2016; Singha et al., 2012), an orthologue of the Tim22 subunit of the TIM22 complex (Žárský and Doležal, 2016; Pyrihová et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to phylogenetic studies.

claim: The PAM complex in yeast consists of five essential subunits.
source: In order to translocate presequence-containing proteins, the TIM23 complex must associate with the matrix-localized PAM, which in yeast, consists of five essential subunits (Marom et al., 2011; Schulz et al., 2015; Craig, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on yeast PAM complex.

claim: The five PAM subunits in yeast are mitochondrial heat shock protein 70 (mHsp70), Mge1, Tim44, Pam18, and Pam16.
source: These are (i) the mitochondrial heat shock protein 70 (mHsp70) (Horst et al., 1997; Kang et al., 1990) and (ii) its nucleotide exchange factor Mge1, which mediate the transport of presequence-containing substrates across the mitochondrial membranes; (iii) Tim44 which recruits mHsp70 to Tim23 (Banerjee et al., 2015), the pore-forming subunit of the TIM23 complex.; (iv) Pam18, a J protein with an N-terminal transmembrane domain (TMD) that stimulates ATP hydrolysis of mHsp70 (D'Silva et al., 2003; Truscott et al., 2003; Mokranjac et al., 2006), and is itself regulated by associating with (v) the soluble J-like protein Pam16 (Li et al., 2004; Frazier et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to literature on PAM subunits.

claim: mHsp70 and its nucleotide exchange factor Mge1 mediate the transport of presequence-containing substrates across the mitochondrial membranes.
source: These are (i) the mitochondrial heat shock protein 70 (mHsp70) (Horst et al., 1997; Kang et al., 1990) and (ii) its nucleotide exchange factor Mge1, which mediate the transport of presequence-containing substrates across the mitochondrial membranes
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on mHsp70 function.

claim: Tim44 recruits mHsp70 to Tim23, the pore-forming subunit of the TIM23 complex.
source: (iii) Tim44 which recruits mHsp70 to Tim23 (Banerjee et al., 2015), the pore-forming subunit of the TIM23 complex.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on Tim44 function.

claim: Pam18 is a J protein with an N-terminal transmembrane domain that stimulates ATP hydrolysis of mHsp70.
source: (iv) Pam18, a J protein with an N-terminal transmembrane domain (TMD) that stimulates ATP hydrolysis of mHsp70 (D'Silva et al., 2003; Truscott et al., 2003; Mokranjac et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on Pam18 function.

claim: Pam18 is regulated by associating with the soluble J-like protein Pam16.
source: and is itself regulated by associating with (v) the soluble J-like protein Pam16 (Li et al., 2004; Frazier et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on Pam16-Pam18 interaction.

claim: PAM subunits are relatively well conserved across eukaryotes.
source: These PAM subunits are relatively well conserved across eukaryotes (Fukasawa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a comparative study.

claim: Single trypanosomal orthologues of mHsp70 and Mge1 are readily identified.
source: Single trypanosomal orthologues of mHsp70 and Mge1 are readily identified, and an ORF resembling Tim44 (Tb927.7.4620) is detected through HHPred profile-profile analyses.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis.

claim: An ORF resembling Tim44 (Tb927.7.4620) is detected through HHPred profile-profile analyses in T. brucei.
source: Single trypanosomal orthologues of mHsp70 and Mge1 are readily identified, and an ORF resembling Tim44 (Tb927.7.4620) is detected through HHPred profile-profile analyses.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis using HHPred.

claim: A number of J and J-like proteins are present in the mitochondrial proteome of T. brucei, including putative orthologues of Pam16 and 18.
source: Furthermore, a number of J and J-like proteins are present in the mitochondrial proteome of T. brucei, including putative orthologues of Pam 16 and 18 (Fukasawa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a proteomics study.

claim: TbPam27 is an essential component of the trypanosomal PAM.
source: Instead, we show that the J protein TbPam27 is an essential component of the trypanosomal PAM.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: TbPam27 convergently evolved to replace the function of the ancestral Pam18 in kinetoplastids.
source: This suggests that TbPam27 convergently evolved to replace the function of the ancestral Pam18 in kinetoplastids, probably via neutral evolutionary processes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings, involving speculation about evolutionary processes.

claim: The protein similarity network identified four clusters corresponding to putative PAM subunits.
source: We identified four clusters in this network that correspond to putative PAM subunits and selected them for further experimental analyses (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis shown in figures.

claim: Two clusters correspond to the Pam16 and Pam18 subfamilies of J proteins found in diverse eukaryotic representatives, including euglenozoans.
source: Two clusters correspond to the Pam16 and Pam18 subfamilies of J proteins which are found in diverse eukaryotic representatives, including euglenozoans (e.g., kinetoplastids, diplonemids and euglenids).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: TbPam27 (Tb927.10.13830) is a 27 kDa protein previously found to be associated with the single trypanosomal TIM complex.
source: One was of special interest since its member in T. brucei is a 27 kDa protein (Tb927.10.13830, termed TbPam27) previously found to be associated with the single trypanosomal TIM complex (Harsman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Tb927.4.650 is a kinetoplastid-specific J protein that appeared closest in similarity to Pam18 and Pam16 in profile Hidden Markov Model searches.
source: Finally, our analysis revealed another kinetoplastid-specific cluster whose member in T. brucei is Tb927.4.650 and which appeared closest in similarity to Pam18 and Pam16 in profile Hidden Markov Model (HMM) searches.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis.

claim: T. brucei has orthologues of Pam16 (Tb927.9.13530) and Pam18 (Tb927.8.6310).
source: Thus, our network and phylogenetic analysis (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2) of J proteins confirms that T. brucei has not only orthologues of Pam16 (Tb927.9.13530, termed TbPam16) and Pam18 (Tb927.8.6310, termed TbPam18) (Fukasawa et al., 2017)
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis and supported by citation.

claim: TbPam27, TbPam18, TbPam16, and Tb927.4.650 co-fractionate with the mitochondrial marker ATOM40 in digitonin extractions.
source: Cell extractions with low concentration of digitonin show that the four C-terminally epitope-tagged proteins co-fractionate with the mitochondrial marker ATOM40 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: TbPam27, TbPam18, TbPam16, and Tb927.4.650 are present in the mitochondrial proteome defined by ImportOmics.
source: Moreover, the four proteins are all present in the mitochondrial proteome defined by ImportOmics (Peikert et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a proteomics study.

claim: TbPam27, TbPam18, TbPam16, and Tb927.4.650 are integral membrane proteins.
source: All proteins are also exclusively recovered in the pellet when a crude mitochondrial fraction is subjected to carbonate extraction at high pH, suggesting they are integral membrane proteins (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by carbonate extraction experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: TbPam27, TbPam18 and TbPam16 are localized inside a membrane-bound compartment.
source: Protease protection experiments additionally show that TbPam27, TbPam18 and TbPam16 remain intact in crude mitochondrial fractions and are only digested when the membrane barrier is destroyed by detergent. This indicates that all three tagged proteins are localized inside a membrane-bound compartment (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by protease protection assays shown in Figure 2C.

claim: TbPam27 is assigned to the mitochondrial inner membrane based on normalized abundance profiles.
source: Finally, normalized abundance profiles of TbPam27 over six subcellular fractions, produced in a previous proteomic analysis (Niemann et al., 2013), assign it to the mitochondrial inner membrane (IM) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on proteomic data from a previous study shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Immunoprecipitation experiments using tagged TbPam27 as bait efficiently recover the TIM subunits TbTim17 and TimRhom I.
source: Immunoprecipitation (IP) experiments, in which tagged TbPam27 is used as the bait, efficiently recovers the TIM subunits TbTim17 and TimRhom I (Figure 3A, left most panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Immunoprecipitation experiments using tagged TbPam18, TbPam16 or Tb927.4.650 as baits do not recover TIM subunits.
source: However, the same is not the case when tagged TbPam18, TbPam16 or Tb927.4.650 are used as baits (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: TbPam27 was efficiently enriched in three out of four SILAC-IP experiments using TIM subunits as baits.
source: Interestingly, TbPam27 was efficiently enriched in three out of four experiments.
evidence: This is based on SILAC-IP data summarized in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: TbPam18, TbPam16 and Tb927.4.650 were either not detected or not enriched in SILAC-IP experiments using TIM subunits as baits.
source: TbPam18, TbPam16 and Tb927.4.650, however, were either not detected in any of the four experiments, or in the case of TbPam16, in the ACAD pull down experiment, not enriched.
evidence: This is based on SILAC-IP data summarized in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: TbPam27, but not TbPam18, TbPam16 or Tb927.4.650, is associated with the trypanosomal TIM.
source: Thus, TbPam27, but not TbPam18, TbPam16 or Tb927.4.650, is associated with the trypanosomal TIM.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple IP and SILAC-IP experiments.

claim: In the TbPam16-HA SILAC-IP, TbPam18 was the protein most enriched besides the bait (5.7-fold).
source: For TbPam16, the protein that was enriched the most and significantly detected, besides the bait, was TbPam18 (5.7-fold), suggesting that the two proteins interact.
evidence: This is based on SILAC-IP data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: None of the eight detected TIM subunits was enriched in the TbPam16-HA SILAC-IP.
source: Most importantly, however, neither of the eight detected TIM subunits was enriched (Figure 3B, left panel; Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is based on SILAC-IP data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In the TbPam18-HA SILAC-IP, proteins with the highest significant enrichment are either annotated as ER proteins or predicted to be involved in ER-related processes.
source: Unexpectedly, essentially all the proteins with the highest significant enrichment are either annotated as ER proteins or predicted to be involved in ER-related processes, such as glycosylation or glycosyl-phosphatidyl inositol (GPI) anchoring.
evidence: This is based on SILAC-IP data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The 11 detected TIM subunits show only marginal enrichment (1.6–1.8-fold) in the TbPam18-HA SILAC-IP.
source: Of all the detected mitochondrial proteins, in contrast, only TbPam18 itself was enriched more than 3-fold, and the 11 detected TIM subunits show only a marginal enrichment of 1.6–1.8-fold, considering the 26.3-fold enrichment of the bait.
evidence: This is based on SILAC-IP data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: TbPam16 was not detected in the TbPam18-HA SILAC-IP.
source: TbPam16 was not detected, which suggests that the C-terminal tag of TbPam18 might prevent the interaction between the two proteins.
evidence: This is based on SILAC-IP data and involves inference about tag effects.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation using the stuck LDH-DHFR substrate as bait recovers TbPam27-myc along with ATOM40, TbTim17 and TimRhom I.
source: Figure 4A shows that CoIP experiments using the stuck substrate in the presence of aminopterin as the bait, not only recover the LDH-DHFR-HA along with ATOM40 and the TIM components TbTim17 and TimRhom I, as expected, but also the myc-tagged TbPam27.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation using TbPam27-myc as bait precipitates LDH-DHFR-HA, ATOM40, TbTim17 and TimRhom I.
source: Moreover, the reverse experiment, using TbPam27-myc as the bait, precipitates the very same proteins LDH-DHFR-HA, ATOM40, TbTim17 and TimRhom I.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Only negligible amounts of VDAC were recovered in co-immunoprecipitation experiments with the stuck presequence substrate or TbPam27.
source: However, only negligible amounts of the OM protein VDAC, which was used as a control, were recovered in either of the two experiments.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Only marginal amounts of TbPam27-HA were recovered when MCP12ΔI-myc was used as bait in co-immunoprecipitation.
source: IP experiments in Figure 4B using anti-myc antibodies, show that TbTim17 was efficiently co-precipitated with MCP12ΔI-myc, but that only marginal amounts of TbPam27-HA were recovered in the eluate.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: TimRhom I and Cox IV remained in the unbound fraction when MCP12ΔI-myc was used as bait in co-immunoprecipitation.
source: Moreover, as expected, the presequence translocase-specific TimRhom I, as well as cytochrome oxidase subunit 4 (Cox IV), remained in the unbound fraction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation using TbPam27-HA as bait efficiently precipitated TbTim17 and TimRhom I, but not MCP12ΔI-myc and Cox IV.
source: Conversely, IP using TbPam27-HA efficiently precipitated TbTim17 and TimRhom I, whereas MCP12ΔI-myc and Cox IV were not recovered.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: TbPam27 is much higher enriched in the presequence rather than the carrier translocase SILAC-IP.
source: The figure illustrates that TbPam27 is much higher enriched in the presequence rather than the carrier translocase SILAC-IP.
evidence: This is based on SILAC-IP data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: TbPam16 and TbPam18 are either not detected or enriched to a lesser extent than VDAC in presequence and carrier translocase SILAC-IPs.
source: Moreover, TbPam16 and TbPam18 are either not detected in these experiments or enriched to a lesser extent than the control protein VDAC.
evidence: This is based on SILAC-IP data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: TbPam27, but neither TbPam16 nor TbPam18, is specifically associated with the active presequence translocase.
source: In summary, these experiments show that TbPam27, but neither TbPam16 nor TbPam18, is specifically associated with the active presequence translocase.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple co-IP and SILAC-IP experiments.

claim: Ablation of TbPam27 causes a rapid growth arrest.
source: Figure 5A, left panel shows that ablation of TbPam27 causes a rapid growth arrest and a concomitant accumulation of unprocessed Cox IV.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Ablation of TbPam27 causes accumulation of unprocessed Cox IV.
source: Figure 5A, left panel shows that ablation of TbPam27 causes a rapid growth arrest and a concomitant accumulation of unprocessed Cox IV.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The levels of TbTim17 are not affected by ablation of TbPam27.
source: Importantly, the levels of TbTim17, one of the core subunits of the trypanosomal TIM complex, are not affected.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis in Figure 5A.

claim: Accumulation of precursor Cox IV indicates that mitochondrial import of presequence-containing proteins is inhibited.
source: Previous work has shown that accumulation of precursor Cox IV indicates that mitochondrial import of presequence-containing proteins is inhibited (Peikert et al., 2017; Pusnik et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ablation of TbmHsp70 causes a rapid growth arrest and accumulation of unprocessed Cox IV.
source: Essentially identical results as for TbPam27 RNAi were obtained when the analogous experiment was done for the single trypanosomal mitochondrial heat shock protein 70 (TbmHsp70).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: TbmHsp70 is required for matrix protein import.
source: TbmHsp70, as shown before, is required for matrix protein import (Tschopp et al., 2011; Figure 5A, right panels).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study and data in Figure 5A.

claim: TbPam27 and TbmHsp70 are essential for growth.
source: These results show that TbPam27 and TbmHsp70 are essential for growth and that their function is linked to mitochondrial protein import.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on RNAi experiments.

claim: The function of TbPam27 and TbmHsp70 is linked to mitochondrial protein import.
source: These results show that TbPam27 and TbmHsp70 are essential for growth and that their function is linked to mitochondrial protein import.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on RNAi experiments showing Cox IV precursor accumulation.

claim: Ectopic expression of wildtype TbPam27 in the 5' UTR RNAi cell line restores growth to nearly wild-type levels.
source: The left panels in Figure 5B show that, as expected, ectopic expression of untagged TbPam27 in the 5' UTR RNAi cell line restores growth to nearly wild-type levels and prevents Cox IV precursor accumulation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by complementation experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Ectopic expression of wildtype TbPam27 in the 5' UTR RNAi cell line prevents Cox IV precursor accumulation.
source: The left panels in Figure 5B show that, as expected, ectopic expression of untagged TbPam27 in the 5' UTR RNAi cell line restores growth to nearly wild-type levels and prevents Cox IV precursor accumulation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by complementation experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A variant of TbPam27 containing a H77Q substitution in the J domain does not complement the TbPam27 RNAi phenotype.
source: However, when the same experiment was performed with a variant of TbPam27 containing a single H to Q substitution at position 77 in the conserved HPD motif of the J domain, no complementation was observed (Figure 5B, right panels).
evidence: This is demonstrated by complementation experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: TbPam27 requires an intact J domain to exert its function.
source: Thus, TbPam27, as yeast and human Pam18, but unlike Pam16, requires an intact J domain to exert its function.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on complementation experiments with the H77Q mutant.

claim: In yeast and humans, Pam18, but not Pam16, requires an intact J domain for its function.
source: In yeast and humans, Pam18, but not Pam16, requires an intact J domain for its function (D'Silva et al., 2003; Davey et al., 2006; Sinha et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on yeast and human Pam proteins.

claim: TbPam27 is essential for normal growth of T. brucei bloodstream forms.
source: The result in Figure 5C shows that TbPam27, indeed, is also essential for normal growth of T. brucei bloodstream forms.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi experiments in bloodstream form cells shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Ablation of TbPam18 causes a growth arrest.
source: Figure 6A shows that ablation of TbPam18 and TbPam16 causes a growth arrest and an accumulation of unprocessed Cox IV.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Ablation of TbPam16 causes a growth arrest.
source: Figure 6A shows that ablation of TbPam18 and TbPam16 causes a growth arrest and an accumulation of unprocessed Cox IV.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Ablation of TbPam18 causes accumulation of unprocessed Cox IV two days after the growth phenotype became apparent.
source: However, unlike for TbPam27, precursor accumulation was only observed two days after the growth phenotype became apparent, suggesting that it is an indirect effect.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Ablation of TbPam16 causes accumulation of unprocessed Cox IV two days after the growth phenotype became apparent.
source: However, unlike for TbPam27, precursor accumulation was only observed two days after the growth phenotype became apparent, suggesting that it is an indirect effect.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Ablation of Tb927.4.650 affected cell-growth only slightly and caused no Cox IV precursor accumulation.
source: Ablation of Tb927.4.650, on the other hand, affected cell-growth only slightly and caused no Cox IV precursor accumulation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 6A.

claim: TbPam18 is not essential for normal growth of the bloodstream form of T. brucei.
source: The results in Figure 6B show that, in contrast to what was seen for TbPam27 (Figure 5C), this is not the case.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi experiments in bloodstream form cells shown in Figure 6B.

claim: TbPam16 is not essential for normal growth of the bloodstream form of T. brucei.
source: The results in Figure 6B show that, in contrast to what was seen for TbPam27 (Figure 5C), this is not the case.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi experiments in bloodstream form cells shown in Figure 6B.

claim: TbPam16 and TbPam18 do not have an essential function in mitochondrial protein import.
source: This result indicates that neither TbPam18 nor TbPam16 have an essential function in mitochondrial protein import.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the lack of essentiality in bloodstream forms.

claim: The essential functions of TbPam16 and TbPam18 are limited to the procyclic form.
source: Thus, while we do not know what the essential functions of TbPam16 and TbPam18 are, they are limited to the procyclic form.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on differential essentiality between life cycle stages.

claim: TbPam16 and TbPam18 are not recruited to the TIM complex in the absence of TbPam27.
source: Moreover, CoIP experiments, in which TbPam18-HA or TbPam16-HA in TbPam27 depleted cells were used as baits, still do not recover the TIM subunits TbTim17 or TimRhom I (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TbPam18 and TbPam16 are not associated with the TIM complex, irrespectively whether TbPam27 is present or not.
source: Thus, TbPam18 and TbPam16 are not associated with the TIM complex, irrespectively whether TbPam27 is present or not.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on co-IP experiments in TbPam27-depleted cells.

claim: Formation of the stalled presequence pathway intermediate depends on an active PAM module.
source: Formation of the stalled presequence pathway intermediate (Figure 4A) in the presence of aminopterin is expected to depend on an active PAM module (Schulz and Rehling, 2014), which pulls the unfolded moiety of the LDH-DHFR-myc precursor across the ATOM and the TIM complexes into the matrix.
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on PAM function.

claim: Formation of the carrier intermediate should be independent of the PAM module.
source: Formation of the carrier intermediate, however, should be independent of the PAM module (Chacinska et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on carrier import.

claim: LDH-DHFR-myc accumulates in a high molecular weight complex corresponding to the import intermediate stuck in the import complexes.
source: Blue native (BN)-PAGE analysis demonstrates that LDH-DHFR-myc accumulates in a high molecular weight complex corresponding to the import intermediate that is stuck in the import complexes as shown in the left panel of Figure 7A.
evidence: This is demonstrated by BN-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Complex formation of the stalled presequence intermediate is largely abolished in induced TbPam27 RNAi cells after growth arrest becomes apparent.
source: However, complex formation is largely abolished in induced TbPam27 RNAi cells after the time point, when the arrest in growth becomes apparent.
evidence: This is demonstrated by BN-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Complex formation of the stalled presequence intermediate is largely abolished in induced TbmHsp70 RNAi cells.
source: As a positive control, the analogous experiment was done in a TbmHsp70 RNAi cell line, and essentially the same result was obtained (Figure 7A, right panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by BN-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: TbPam27 and TbmHsp70 are required for the formation of the stalled presequence pathway intermediate.
source: These results demonstrate that both, TbPam27 and TbmHsp70, are required for the formation of the stalled presequence pathway intermediate.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on BN-PAGE analysis of import intermediates.

claim: Accumulation of the truncated MCP12ΔI-myc at the TIM complex was not affected by ablation of TbPam27 for at least 2 days.
source: Interestingly, accumulation of the truncated MCP12ΔI-myc at the TIM complex was not affected by ablation of TbPam27 for at least 2 days (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by BN-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Ablation of TbPam27 selectively interferes with the formation of the stalled presequence intermediate but not with formation of the carrier intermediate.
source: Thus, as expected for a PAM subunit, ablation of TbPam27 selectively interferes with the formation of the stalled presequence intermediate but not with formation of the carrier intermediate (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on BN-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 7B and 7C.

claim: Ablation of TbPam18 does not interfere with the formation of the import arrested presequence-containing substrate.
source: Figure 8 shows that ablation of neither of the two proteins interferes with the formation of the import arrested presequence-containing substrate.
evidence: This is demonstrated by BN-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Ablation of TbPam16 does not interfere with the formation of the import arrested presequence-containing substrate.
source: Figure 8 shows that ablation of neither of the two proteins interferes with the formation of the import arrested presequence-containing substrate.
evidence: This is demonstrated by BN-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: 899 mitochondrial proteins were detected in the TbPam27 RNAi SILAC experiment, corresponding to 83% of the previously determined proteome.
source: We detected 899 mitochondrial proteins, which corresponds to 83% of the previously determined proteome (Peikert et al., 2017), and of which 34.4% are downregulated more the 1.5-fold. (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is based on quantitative MS data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: 34.4% of detected mitochondrial proteins are downregulated more than 1.5-fold after TbPam27 ablation.
source: We detected 899 mitochondrial proteins, which corresponds to 83% of the previously determined proteome (Peikert et al., 2017), and of which 34.4% are downregulated more the 1.5-fold. (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is based on quantitative MS data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: 66.5% of all detected mitochondrial proteins contain predicted mitochondrial presequences.
source: Of all detected mitochondrial proteins, 66.5% contain predicted mitochondrial presequences (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic prediction and MS data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: 39.6% of presequence-containing proteins show more than 1.5-fold decreased steady-state levels 1.5 days after TbPam27 RNAi induction.
source: 39.6% of the presequence-containing proteins show more than 1.5-fold decreased steady-state levels 1.5 days after TbPam27 RNAi induction.
evidence: This is based on quantitative MS data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: 24.6% of mitochondrial proteins without presequences (excluding carrier proteins) are reduced more than 1.5-fold after TbPam27 ablation.
source: However, only 24.6% of the remaining mitochondrial proteins, that presumably have internal targeting sequences (excluding the 12 detected carrier proteins), are reduced more than 1.5-fold (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is based on quantitative MS data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Only one of 12 detected mitochondrial carrier proteins is more than 1.5-fold downregulated (8.3%) after TbPam27 ablation.
source: Finally, looking specifically at the mitochondrial carrier proteins, we found that only one of them is more than 1.5-fold downregulated (8.3%) (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is based on quantitative MS data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Ablation of TbPam27 preferentially affects the presequence pathway.
source: In summary, these experiments show that ablation of TbPam27, as expected for a PAM subunit, preferentially affects the presequence pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on quantitative MS data showing differential effects on protein classes.

claim: Ablation of TbPam27 does not affect the levels of TIM complex subunits.
source: The results also demonstrate that ablation of TbPam27 does not affect the levels of TIM complex subunits (Figure 9—figure supplement 1), indicating that the trypanosomal TIM complex and the putative PAM complex are separate entities.
evidence: This is based on quantitative MS data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: The trypanosomal TIM complex and the putative PAM complex are separate entities.
source: The results also demonstrate that ablation of TbPam27 does not affect the levels of TIM complex subunits (Figure 9—figure supplement 1), indicating that the trypanosomal TIM complex and the putative PAM complex are separate entities.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that PAM ablation doesn't affect TIM levels.

claim: TbPam27 is an essential mitochondrial inner membrane protein.
source: Here, we show that TbPam27 is an essential mitochondrial IM protein.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from localization and RNAi experiments.

claim: TbPam27 is associated with the presequence translocase but not with the carrier translocase version of the trypanosomal TIM.
source: It is associated with the presequence translocase but not with the carrier translocase version of the trypanosomal TIM and functions analogously to fungal Pam18.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from co-IP and import intermediate experiments.

claim: TbPam27 functions analogously to fungal Pam18.
source: It is associated with the presequence translocase but not with the carrier translocase version of the trypanosomal TIM and functions analogously to fungal Pam18.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on functional similarities.

claim: Like Pam18, TbPam27 is an integral inner membrane protein.
source: Like Pam18, TbPam27 is an integral IM protein and requires an intact J domain for its function.
evidence: This is based on carbonate extraction and complementation experiments.

claim: Like Pam18, TbPam27 requires an intact J domain for its function.
source: Like Pam18, TbPam27 is an integral IM protein and requires an intact J domain for its function.
evidence: This is based on complementation experiments with the H77Q mutant.

claim: Unlike Pam18 subfamily members which have N-terminal TMDs, TbPam27 is C-terminally anchored in the inner membrane.
source: However, unlike Pam18 subfamily members, which have N-terminal TMDs, TbPam27 is C-terminally anchored in the IM membrane.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and comparison.

claim: The J domain of TbPam27 has a reverse orientation relative to the inner membrane when compared to Pam18 of yeast and humans.
source: Consequently, the J domain of TbPam27 has a reverse orientation relative to the IM when compared to Pam18 of yeast and humans (Mokranjac et al., 2006).
evidence: This is inferred from the C-terminal anchoring of TbPam27 versus N-terminal anchoring of Pam18.

claim: Trichomonas and Giardia Pam18s localize to hydrogenosomes and mitosomes, respectively.
source: There are some data which show that Trichomonas and Giardia Pam18s localize to hydrogenosomes and mitosomes, respectively (Rada et al., 2011; Dolezal et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on these organisms.

claim: The J domain of Trichomonas Pam18 can complement the J domain of S. cerevisiae Pam18.
source: A rudimentary functional conservation has been demonstrated as the J domain of the Trichomonas Pam18 can complement the J domain of S. cerevisiae Pam18 (Rada et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a functional study.

claim: The PAM subunit Tim44 has orthologues in essentially all eukaryotes including Trichomonas and Giardia.
source: The PAM subunit Tim44 has orthologues in essentially all eukaryotes (Clements et al., 2009) including Trichomonas and Giardia (Pyrihová et al., 2018; Rada et al., 2011; Martincová et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to comparative studies.

claim: Trypanosomes lack a clear Tim44 orthologue.
source: Trypanosomes, on the other hand, lack a clear Tim44 orthologue (Pyrihová et al., 2018; Martincová et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to comparative studies.

claim: A protein whose C-terminal domain shows similarity to Tim44 by HHPred has been identified in T. brucei but is not associated with the trypanosomal TIM complex.
source: A protein, whose C-terminal domain shows similarity to Tim44 by HHPred has been identified in T. brucei. However, it has been shown that this protein is not associated with the trypanosomal TIM complex (Harsman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: T. brucei retains orthologues of Pam16 and Pam18 in its mitochondrion.
source: Surprisingly, T. brucei retains orthologues of Pam16 and Pam 18 in its mitochondrion.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis presented in the study.

claim: TbPam16 and TbPam18 are not subunits of the trypanosomal PAM.
source: However, we show that neither of the two proteins is associated with the TIM complex, nor does their ablation interfere with the formation of the presequence pathway intermediate. Furthermore, unlike TbPam27, they are not essential for the bloodstream form of T. brucei. These data indicate that they are not subunits of the trypanosomal PAM.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental approaches.

claim: The ancestral function of Pam18 has likely been taken over by TbPam27.
source: Instead, the ancestral function of Pam18 has likely been taken over by TbPam27.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on functional data showing TbPam27 performs Pam18-like functions.

claim: Previous examples of convergent evolution for the mitochondrial protein import system of T. brucei include ATOM46, ATOM69, and pATOM36.
source: Previous examples of convergent evolution for the mitochondrial protein import system of T. brucei have been described. They include the two OM import receptors ATOM46 and ATOM69 (Mani et al., 2015) as well as pATOM36 (Vitali et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LECA most likely already had both TIM23 and TIM22 complexes.
source: Previous work has shown that LECA most likely already had both, TIM23 and TIM22 complexes (Fukasawa et al., 2017; Žárský and Doležal, 2016; Pyrihová et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to evolutionary studies.

claim: A neutral replacement of the ancestral Pam18, and possibly also Pam16, by TbPam27 took place in an ancestor of the kinetoplastids.
source: We suggest that a neutral replacement of the ancestral Pam18, and possibly also Pam16, by TbPam27 took place in an ancestor of the kinetoplastids, or even possibly at the dawn of the Glycomonada (Kinetoplastea and Diplonemea), as an orthologue of TbPam27 is found in Diplonema sp. (Cavalier-Smith, 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary scenario based on phylogenetic distribution.

claim: An orthologue of TbPam27 is found in Diplonema sp.
source: We suggest that a neutral replacement of the ancestral Pam18, and possibly also Pam16, by TbPam27 took place in an ancestor of the kinetoplastids, or even possibly at the dawn of the Glycomonada (Kinetoplastea and Diplonemea), as an orthologue of TbPam27 is found in Diplonema sp. (Cavalier-Smith, 2016).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis and supported by citation.

claim: TbTim17 is most closely related to Tim22, which forms the pore of the TIM22 complex.
source: TbTim17, a T. brucei TIM core subunit, is most closely related to Tim22, which forms the pore of the TIM22 complex (Žárský and Doležal, 2016; Pyrihová et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to phylogenetic studies.

claim: TimRhom I and TimRhom II are specifically associated with the presequence translocase.
source: TimRhom I and TimRhom II are specifically associated with the presequence translocase (Harsman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The recruitment of TimRhom I and TimRhom II as auxiliary components may have facilitated the import of presequence-containing proteins and promoted the transition to a single TIM complex.
source: The recruitment of these proteins as auxiliary components that facilitate the import of presequence-containing proteins, may have further promoted the transition to a single TIM complex (Figure 10D).
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary scenario illustrated in Figure 10.

claim: TbPam16 and TbPam18 were retained because they either acquired a new function or hold an overlooked ancestral role.
source: TbPam18 and TbPam16 were retained because they either acquired a new as yet unknown function, or hold an overlooked ancestral role.
evidence: This is speculation about why these proteins are retained.

claim: Unlike its yeast homologue, TbPam18 seems to be dually localized in the ER and in mitochondria.
source: Interestingly, unlike its yeast homologue, TbPam18 seems to be dually localized in the ER and in mitochondria.
evidence: This is based on SILAC-IP data showing enrichment of ER proteins.

claim: Retention of both TbPam16 and TbPam18 in all kinetoplastids provides constraints regarding their possible function.
source: Moreover, retention of both proteins in all kinetoplastids and the fact that their RNAi-mediated ablation in T. brucei specifically interferes with growth of the procyclic but not the bloodstream forms provides both, further information and constraints regarding their possible function.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic distribution and differential essentiality data.
